SASRec’s original ablations separately remove LayerNorm, positional embeddings, and residual connections; they do not establish that a gated recent-item mean residual improves recency modeling. Its implementation also scales input embeddings by √d. Recommended controls: cross residual on/off with normalization unchanged/modified; preserve embedding scaling, optimizer, sampling, and training budget. Compare recent-window pooling with last-item, full-history mean, and equally sized older-window pooling. Measure branch norms and gate values to detect scale effects. These are proposed controls, informed by [SASRec](https://arxiv.org/html/1808.09781) and its [implementation](https://recommenders-team.github.io/recommenders/_modules/recommenders/models/sasrec/model.html).

Repeated consumption is a separate mechanism: [RepeatNet](https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/4408) explicitly separates repeat and explore predictions, with larger gains on higher-repeat datasets. Diagnose target-in-history frequency and report validation results separately for repeated versus unseen targets, where present, without changing evaluator candidates. Compare occurrence-weighted pooling against pooling unique recent item IDs; disappearance of gains suggests duplicate amplification. Full-catalog unseen-item recommendations cannot benefit from directly recommending a previously consumed ID, although repeated history can still distort representations.

Recency can also conflict with purchase timing. [Scalable Demand-Aware Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.06347) models reduced demand shortly after a purchase within a durable-goods category, using category-specific replacement intervals. Here, fine-grained categories and ownership are unavailable: broad dataset routing cannot establish saturation. Use timestamp-gap and repeat-frequency strata as descriptive checks, retaining all four datasets and macro validation HR@10. Interaction timestamps alone cannot identify purchase completion, replacement need, or causal satiation; weak recent-item gains are evidence of predictive limitations, not proof of durable-goods saturation.
